hero.lede: Czechia is a top-tier manufacturing nation and has the 7th most complex economy in the world. However, its wealth is growing at only an average rate. The Pirate Expert Economic Council (PEER) has drawn up a plan to accelerate growth by 1 percentage point a year. This page summarises its main ideas for readers outside Czechia.
hero.bobr: We, the authors of the strategy, know that one percentage point may not sound like much. But over ten years, it amounts to CZK 1,000 billion a year.

numbers.label: one percentage point faster economic growth each year
higher annual economic output at the end of the decade
extra in wages per worker per year, on average

topics.title: Housing where the opportunities are
topics.hook: How many years’ salary does a flat cost?
topics.label: Czechia, a new average flat, 2025
topics.lede: The highest in the whole of the European Union. The average is between 8 and 10. In Belgium, it is just under 5.
topics.role: economist and academic, lead expert on affordable housing and modern infrastructure

topics.title: Education as the foundation of economic prosperity
topics.hook: Why isn’t it worth skimping on nursery schools?
topics.unit: of children under 3 years of age
topics.label: attends a crèche, nursery or playgroup
topics.lede: The OECD average is 24%. The EU’s target is 45% by 2030. Every koruna invested in early childhood care yields a return of 3–4 times that amount for the state.
topics.role: expert in education for the future and strong regions

topics.title: From the assembly line to the economy of smart people
topics.hook: Why is cheap labour a trap here?
topics.label: 43% of the average wage, lower than in Poland, Lithuania and Croatia
topics.lede: The average wage is only 60–65% of the EU average. Yet up to 80% of people on the minimum wage are entitled to benefits, meaning that the state ends up subsidising these low wages. In 2023, only 0.005% of GDP was spent on retraining, whilst the OECD average is 0.1%.
topics.role: expert on labour market mobilisation and equal opportunities

topics.title: Women in the labour market: the greatest untapped potential
topics.hook: Why has Poland overtaken us in terms of wages?
topics.label: between men and women, the second highest in the EU
topics.lede: Polish and Lithuanian women earn more than Czech women. In the public sector, the pay gap stands at 17% – the highest in the EU. Every 1% reduction in the pay gap in the private sector adds CZK 4.9 billion to the budget each year.
topics.role: expert on labour market mobilisation and equal opportunities

topics.title: Debt enforcement: a system that punishes work and destroys children’s futures
topics.hook: Why isn’t it worth it for half a million people to work?
topics.unit: people subject to debt enforcement proceedings
topics.label: as at 30 June 2026; 3 million cases, CZK 542 billion
topics.lede: Anyone earning more than approximately CZK 31,500 gross will lose every additional koruna. Debts are falling by just 1% a year, and only through the write-off of irrecoverable debts.
topics.role: expert on labour market mobilisation and equal opportunities

topics.title: Health and self-sufficiency
topics.hook: How much does it cost us to be ill?
topics.label: economic loss due to poor health and premature deaths (~14% of GDP)
topics.lede: Men in Czechia can expect to live 61.2 years in good health. In Sweden, the figure is around 71. Yet 62% of the healthy years lost are among people of working age.
topics.role: economist and manager, former Deputy Minister of Health; responsible for the ‘Healthy Nation’ and ‘Sustainable Pensions’ sections

topics.title: Weakening the oligarchy and fair subsidies
topics.hook: Who receives the subsidies that we all pay for?
topics.label: in substantial subsidies goes to the biggest players
topics.lede: Research by CERGE-EI shows that these subsidies do not lead to greater innovation or productivity, but rather to increased profits for these firms.
topics.role: academic; responsible for the chapters on a fair market, smart taxes and sustainable finance

topics.title: Adoption of the euro
topics.hook: Why do Czechs pay CZK 1.2 million more than Slovaks for the same mortgage?
topics.label: in additional interest payments, a 30-year mortgage of CZK 4.7 million, Czechia compared with Slovakia
topics.lede: The same bank, the same product, a three-year fixed-rate period. A rate of 4.94% in Czechia compared with 3.69% in Slovakia.
topics.role: economist, specialising in European integration and the euro

topics.title: Czech capital lying dormant
topics.hook: What does your money get up to whilst you’re asleep?
topics.label: the dormant savings of Czech savers
topics.lede: This money is not usually put to work and a significant proportion of it sits in non-interest-bearing current accounts.
topics.role: academic; responsible for the chapters on a fair market, smart taxes and sustainable finance

topics.title: From an assembly plant to our own product
topics.hook: We produce like the elite. Why are we getting rich like the average person?
topics.label: paid out abroad in dividends in 2025
topics.lede: Czechia is the 7th most complex economy in the world according to the Economic Complexity Index, but in terms of GDP per capita we rank around 40th. Profits made by foreign owners amounted to CZK 602 billion, or 7% of GDP.
topics.role: expert in modern industry and energy security

topics.title: Energy for the future
topics.hook: Where do hundreds of billions go every year?
topics.label: went abroad in 2025 to buy coal, oil and gas
topics.lede: In terms of purchasing power, Czech households pay the second-highest electricity prices in the EU. Every kilowatt-hour generated from domestic sources reduces that bill.
topics.role: expert in modern industry and energy security

topics.title: Innovation as the driving force behind a strong economy
topics.hook: Why are so few companies being set up here?
topics.label: Czechia
topics.lede: Israel has 410. Austria has twice as many as we do. Even Hungary has overtaken us.
topics.role: entrepreneur and investor, championing the areas of the digital state, AI and efficient institutions

topics.title: Successful regions and effective local government
topics.hook: How much of the local economy will remain within the municipality?
topics.label: Czechia: proportion of local authorities’ revenue derived from the local economy
topics.lede: Within the EU, only Greece is worse off. The EU average is between 20 and 25%.
topics.role: expert in education for the future and strong regions

topics.title: The state as a leader
topics.hook: How many government services can you carry out online?
topics.unit: of public services are fully digital
topics.label: out of a total of nearly 9,000 services
topics.lede: Around 30% of services are hybrid, whilst more than half remain on paper. Software tools for the SZIF (State Agricultural Intervention Fund) cost up to 20 times more than they would have in the commercial sector.
topics.role: entrepreneur and investor, championing the areas of the digital state, AI and efficient institutions

about: The Economic Strategy 2026–2035 was drawn up by the Pirate Expert Economic Council (PEER) in collaboration with the Institut π and other experts. The Council comprises economists, academics and businesspeople, each of whom is responsible for several areas of the strategy.

The strategy comprises fourteen chapters and has a single objective: to accelerate the growth of the Czech economy by 1 percentage point per year. According to the study, by the end of the decade this will mean an annual increase in economic output of CZK 1,000 billion, an additional CZK 300 billion per year in the state budget, and an average of CZK 68,000 per year in additional wages for every economically active person.
The study itself points out that GDP growth cannot be modelled with precision. These figures should be regarded as a target and a rough estimate, rather than as the sum of individual measures.

The strategy was written by people. This website was written, designed and programmed by an artificial intelligence (Claude), which was managed and supervised by a single person. The authors of the strategy, not the website, vouch for the accuracy of the figures. Every figure on the Czech website is accompanied by a source from the study.
site: This is a brief summary in English. The entire website, the ‘Strategy in a minute’ videos, the calculators, the full text of all the chapters and the sources for every figure are in Czech.
